content: Monsanto, a prominent agricultural company, developed and patented the glyphosate molecule in the 1970s. Glyphosate is the active ingredient in the herbicide Roundup, which was first marketed in 1973. Glyphosate is the most widely used herbicide in the United States and holds the record as the best-selling agrichemical of all time. In the U.S., approximately 5-8 million pounds of glyphosate are applied annually to lawns and yards, while 85-90 million pounds are used in agriculture each year. Monsanto retained exclusive rights to glyphosate in the U.S. until its patent expired in September 2000, although it maintained a dominant market share in countries where the patent expired earlier. The active ingredient in Roundup is the isopropylamine salt of glyphosate. Glyphosate works by inhibiting an enzyme essential for the synthesis of the amino acids tyrosine, tryptophan, and phenylalanine. It is absorbed through plant foliage and translocated to growing points, effectively killing actively growing plants. However, weeds and grasses typically re-emerge within one to two months after application. Glyphosate is not effective as a pre-emergence herbicide and only works on actively growing plants. Monsanto also produces genetically engineered seeds, known as Roundup Ready crops, which are tolerant to glyphosate. These seeds contain patented genes that allow farmers to use glyphosate as a post-emergence herbicide to control both broadleaf and cereal weeds. The first Roundup Ready crop was soy, developed at Monsanto's Agracetus Campus in Middleton, Wisconsin. Current Roundup Ready crops include maize (corn), sorghum, cotton, soy, canola, and alfalfa. However, in May 2007, a federal court decision temporarily barred new plantings of Roundup Ready alfalfa and the resale of its seeds due to concerns about environmental impacts, including the potential contamination of non-GM alfalfa crops, the emergence of herbicide-tolerant weeds, and limitations on export markets. Glyphosate is also used by the U.S. government in large quantities to discourage the cultivation of coca plants in South America, as part of initiatives like Plan Colombia. Chemically, glyphosate is an aminophosphonic analogue of the natural amino acid glycine. Its name is derived from glycine, phospho-, and -ate. Glyphosate was discovered to have herbicidal properties in 1970 by John Franz, a Monsanto scientist. Franz received the National Medal of Technology in 1987 and the Perkin Medal for Applied Chemistry in 1990 for his contributions. Biochemically, glyphosate kills plants by inhibiting the enzyme 5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate synthase (EPSPS), which catalyzes a critical reaction in the shikimate pathway. This pathway is essential for the production of aromatic amino acids like phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan, which are precursors for peptides and secondary metabolites such as folates, ubiquinones, and naphthoquinones. X-ray crystallographic studies reveal that glyphosate occupies the binding site of phosphoenolpyruvate, mimicking an intermediate state of the enzyme-substrate complex. The shikimate pathway is absent in animals, which obtain aromatic amino acids from their diet. However, glyphosate has been shown to inhibit other plant enzymes and may also affect animal enzymes. Regarding health and ecological concerns, glyphosate is classified as a moderately toxic herbicide (EPA toxicity class III). A 2000 review concluded that under current and expected conditions of use, Roundup does not pose a health risk to humans. However, this classification has been disputed by organizations like the Northwest Coalition for Alternatives to Pesticides. Glyphosate has been associated with scientific fraud and false advertising. The EPA has caught scientists falsifying test results at research laboratories hired by Monsanto. Additionally, Monsanto has faced lawsuits for misleading advertising of glyphosate products in both the U.S. and Europe. Glyphosate can be lethal if ingested in large quantities, with a mortality rate of approximately 10% for those ingesting Roundup, compared to 70% for paraquat ingestion. Toxicological reviews of Roundup indicate minimal acute and chronic risks to terrestrial non-target organisms but some risks to aquatic organisms in shallow water. Recent research suggests that glyphosate may induce functional abnormalities in fetuses and pregnant rats. It has also been found to interfere with testosterone production in mouse cell cultures and estrogen biosynthesis in human placental cell cultures. Concerns have been raised about its effects on flora, mammals, and birds due to habitat destruction. The U.S. EPA, the EC Health and Consumer Protection Directorate, and the UN World Health Organization have concluded that pure glyphosate is not carcinogenic. However, opponents claim that Roundup has been found to cause genetic damage, which may be attributed to other components in the herbicide mixture rather than glyphosate itself. Glyphosate formulations are more toxic to fish and aquatic invertebrates than to terrestrial organisms. Glyphosate is less persistent in water than in soil, with a persistence of 12 to 60 days in Canadian pond water, but it can persist for over a year in pond sediments in Michigan and Oregon. Roundup is not registered for aquatic use, and studies indicate it is toxic to amphibians. However, glyphosate formulations registered for aquatic use have negligible adverse effects on sensitive amphibians. When glyphosate contacts soil, it binds to soil particles and becomes inactivated. Unbound glyphosate can be degraded by bacteria. Its low activity due to soil binding suggests limited effects on soil flora. However, glyphosate has been described as relatively persistent by the EPA, with soil half-lives ranging from 3 days in Texas to 1-3 years in Swedish forest soils. Northern sites, such as those in Canada and Scandinavia, exhibit longer soil persistence. Glyphosate binding to soil particles can be advantageous, as it allows for complete conversion to non-toxic aminomethylphosphonic acid by immobilized bacteria in industrial wastewater treatment. Glyphosate use may pose risks to endangered plant species and animals like the Houston toad. Some studies suggest effects on earthworm growth and survival, though these findings are inconsistent and have been criticized for methodological flaws. Other studies indicate impaired nitrogen-fixing bacteria and increased crop susceptibility to disease. Monsanto denies any negative impacts and cites studies it has funded to support its position. Concerns have been raised about glyphosate's potential effects on human reproductive health and its classification as an endocrine disruptor. In-vitro studies show that glyphosate affects progesterone production in mammalian cells and placental cell viability. However, whether these findings classify glyphosate as an endocrine disruptor remains debated. Critics argue that in-vitro studies expose cells to unrealistically high concentrations, while proponents believe even small changes in endocrine activity can have lasting effects on organisms. Glyphosate resistance has been documented in weeds, with the first cases reported in Australia. In the U.S., 13 states have reported glyphosate-resistant weeds, posing challenges for farmers reliant on glyphosate for weed control. Resistance has also been observed in microorganisms, with some possessing a version of EPSPS resistant to glyphosate inhibition. This version, isolated from Agrobacterium strain CP4, was engineered into genetically modified crops like soybeans. The CP4 EPSPS gene was fused with a chloroplast transit peptide from petunia EPSPS to ensure proper delivery to plant chloroplasts. The transformation was achieved using particle acceleration, and glyphosate tolerance was tested over multiple generations. Genetically modified soybeans became commercially available in 1996, significantly improving weed control for farmers. Glyphosate-resistant soybean varieties now dominate soybean fields. Glyphosate was first sold under the trade name Roundup by Monsanto, which retains the trademark. However, the chemical formulation is not patented, allowing other manufacturers to produce similar products under various names. Glyphosate is also used by the U.S. government to spray Colombian coca fields as part of Plan Colombia. Its health effects, impact on legal crops, and effectiveness in combating drug cultivation remain widely disputed. The widespread application of glyphosate in South America has led to the development of glyphosate-resistant coca strains, which are larger and higher-yielding than original strains.
